title: Why Amazon would pay up to $7.5B for Israel's Decart
html:
According to Calcalist, Amazon is close to signing its acquisition of Decart, the AI startup founded by Israeli entrepreneurs, possibly as soon as this weekend. According to the report, Amazon is expected to pay more than $7 billion in a mix of cash, stock and deferred payments, with part of the amount tied to targets that could lift it to nearly $7.5 billion. Neither company has confirmed the deal, and until it is signed it could still change.

How did we get here?

Decart's road to Amazon was long. According to Calcalist, its first talks were with Nvidia, which did not renew them after the founders chose to move ahead with another party. Anthropic negotiated a deal of about $6 billion, but according to reports walked away in September after due diligence. Amazon's first offer, in October, was about $5.5 billion according to Calcalist. Since then the price has only risen.

What does Decart do?

The company was founded in 2023 by Dean Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev, who worked together in Unit 8200, along with Orian Leitersdorf. Decart develops software that makes AI chips work more efficiently, running on Nvidia's processors, Amazon's Trainium chips and Google's TPUs. In parallel, it develops models that generate video in real time. According to reports, the three founders have committed to stay at Amazon for five years.

Why does Amazon want it?

The answer starts with chips. Amazon is investing tens of billions of dollars in Trainium, its AI chip, to reduce dependence on Nvidia. The problem is that most AI software was written and tuned for Nvidia's chips, and customers aren't rushing to switch. Software that makes models run well on different chips is exactly the missing link Amazon needs to make Trainium more attractive.

The timing isn't accidental

The deal is coming together in a month when Nvidia lost its founder, Jensen Huang, and the US imposed new chip export controls. Every shock at Nvidia strengthens cloud giants' desire to develop alternatives. Amazon, Google and Microsoft are all competing on the same question: who can build a chip and software that truly compete with Nvidia. Buying Decart is a shortcut in that race.

An open question: what happens to other customers?

Today Decart's software works on both Nvidia chips and Google's TPUs. After an acquisition, Amazon may favor its own chips. If support for rivals' chips shrinks, customers using Decart on other platforms today will need an alternative. That is one of the questions Amazon probably won't answer in its official announcement.

A high price for a young company

GeekWire asked exactly this: why pay billions for a three-year-old company that hasn't disclosed its revenue? The answer is that in the AI market, tech giants aren't buying revenue, they are buying teams and technology that are hard to build quickly. Decart joins a list of acquisitions where the price is set by strategic importance rather than current numbers.

What does it mean for Israeli tech?

If the deal is signed, it will be one of Israel's largest exits of the year, and certainly the largest for such a young company. It comes in a month when Israeli companies from the previous wave, like Firebolt, are selling below their peak valuations, and that is exactly the gap defining Israeli tech today: new AI companies worth billions, and veteran software companies struggling. The next question will be how much of the operation stays in Israel, and at what pace.

The bottom line

Amazon isn't buying Decart for its revenue, but for its place in the big war of the AI era: the war over chips. If Decart's software helps Trainium compete with Nvidia, the price will look cheap. If not, it is another expensive bet in a field where everyone is paying unprecedented prices.
summary: Calcalist reports the deal could be signed within days; analysis of why Decart’s real-time video models matter for Amazon’s Trainium chips.
